source_text: CAPUT VIGESIMUM TERTIUM, De FILIO. Filius est persona secunda in sacrosancta Trinitate, Logos Patris per communicationem eiusdem deitatis, quam Pater habet sine origine, ab aeterno a Patre genitus. Filium dicimus, neque per creationem proprie dictam, quia omnia per illum creata sunt quae creata sunt — Joh. I.3 — neque per adoptionem, quia omnes in illo adoptati sumus qui adoptati filii sumus — Joh. I.12; Eph. I.5-6 — sed per generationem, ut Filium natura, totam divinitatem a Patre communicatam habentem — Mich. V.2. Dicitur Persona eodem significatu quo Pater, quia est subsistens, individuum, incommunicabile — Joh. I — naturae viventis — Joh. V. — intelligentis — Joh. I.18 — volentis — Matth. XI.27; Joh. V.21 — potentis — Phil. III — agentis — Joh. V.17,19. Et quidem persona in sacrosancta Trinitate, hoc est divina, seu, quod idem est, unus et summus ille Deus, Patri et Spiritui sancto coessentialis.
english: The Son is the second person in the most holy Trinity, the Logos of the Father by communication of the same deity which the Father has without origin, begotten from eternity from the Father.

We call Him Son neither by creation properly so called, because all things that were created were created through Him — John 1:3 — nor by adoption, because all who are adopted sons are adopted in Him — John 1:12; Ephesians 1:5-6 — but by generation, as Son by nature, having the whole divinity communicated from the Father — Micah 5:2. He is called Person in the same signification as the Father, because He is a subsistence, individual, incommunicable — John 1 — of living nature — John 5 — understanding — John 1:18 — willing — Matthew 11:27; John 5:21 — powerful — Philippians 3 — acting — John 5:17,19. And indeed a person in the most holy Trinity, that is divine, or, what is the same, that one and highest God, coessential with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

source_text: Hoc quatuor potissimum distinctis argumentorum classibus demonstramus. II. Prima classis est a nominibus Filio a Scriptura tributis. Nam 1. Deus dicitur non solum attributive — Joh. I.1; Rom. IX.5 — verum etiam subjective — I Tim. III.16; Heb. I.8-9; Tit. II.13. 2. Filius Dei dicitur proprie et univoce — Rom. VIII.32; Joh. I.18. 3. Dicitur rex regum et Dominus dominantium, Dominus gloriae — Apoc. XIX.16; I Cor. II.8. IV. Tertia classis est ab operibus divinis. V. Quarta classis est a cultu Dei proprio. VI. Quinta classis est a testimoniis. Ex his bene constitutis colligitur inter Patrem et Filium convenientia et distinctio. Convenientia est in una eademque natura et essentia — Phil. II.6; juxta Nicenam synodum homoousios Patri. Distinctio est in modo subsistendi, quo uterque divinitatem habet. Nam Pater eam habet a nullo, Filius a Patre sibi communicatam.
english: We demonstrate this chiefly by four distinct classes of arguments. II. The first class is from the names attributed to the Son by Scripture. For (1) He is called God not only attributively — John 1:1; Romans 9:5 — but also subjectively — 1 Timothy 3:16; Hebrews 1:8-9; Titus 2:13. (2) He is called Son of God properly and univocally — Romans 8:32; John 1:18. (3) He is called King of kings and Lord of lords, Lord of glory — Revelation 19:16; 1 Corinthians 2:8.
IV. The third class is from divine works. V. The fourth class is from proper worship of God. VI. The fifth class is from testimonies.

From these things well established is gathered agreement and distinction between Father and Son. Agreement is in one and the same nature and essence — Philippians 2:6; according to the Nicene synod homoousios with the Father. Distinction is in the mode of subsisting by which each has divinity. For the Father has it from none, the Son has it communicated to Himself from the Father.

source_text: Quibus frustra oggannit cum Socino suo Johannes Crellius Francus, negans aeternam Filii Dei ex essentia Patris generationem, 1. quia filius foret sui ipsius filius, 2. quia infiniti forent filii, 3. quia Filius Dei ab aeterno et fuisset et non fuisset, 4. quia Filius Dei adhuc generaretur et in omnem aeternitatem generandus esset — quae absurda ex sinistra confusione finitae et infinitae naturae oriuntur. His vero cum Socino suo contradicunt etiam Smalcius, Ostorodius, et ante illos Servetus, Valentinus Gentilis, Alciatus, Blandrata, Franciscus Davidis, horumque omnium patriarchae Photinus episcopus Syrmiensis anno 351 a concilio Syrmiensi damnatus et Paulus Samosatenus. Confer Sozomenum, Epiphanium, Augustinum de haeresibus; e junioribus Urzinum, Calvinum, Zanchium, Junium, Polanum, Tarnovium, Gerhardum; e pontificiis Bellarminum lib. I de Christo cap. 18.
english: Against these things Johannes Crellius the Frenchman, with his Socinus, in vain snarls, denying the eternal generation of the Son of God from the Fathers essence — (1) because the son would be son of himself, (2) because there would be infinite sons, (3) because the Son of God from eternity both would have been and would not have been, (4) because the Son of God would still be being generated and would have to be generated into all eternity — which absurdities arise from a sinister confusion of finite and infinite nature.

To these with his Socinus also contradict Smalcius, Ostorodius, and before them Servetus, Valentinus Gentilis, Alciati, Blandrata, Franciscus Davidis, and the patriarchs of all these, Photinus bishop of Sirmium condemned in the year 351 by the Sirmian council, and Paul of Samosata. Compare Sozomen, Epiphanius, Augustine on heresies; among juniors Ursinus, Calvin, Zanchi, Junius, Polanus, Tarnovius, Gerhard; among pontificals Bellarmine book 1 on Christ chapter 18.

source_text: CAPUT VIGESIMUM TERTIUM, De Spiritu sancto. Spiritus sanctus est tertia persona in sacrosancta Trinitate, quae a Patre emanat, a Filio mittitur, ab utroque secundum hypostasin distincta procedit. Spiritus significat 1. proprie et adaequate ens actu primo et essentia simplicissimum et subtilissimum, actu vero secundo et efficacia maxime activum. Singulari proprietate attribuitur virtuti hypostaticae, seu tertiae personae quae in Deo est, idque non raro cum additamento Spiritus Elohim, Spiritus Domini, Spiritus sanctus — Gen. I.2; Isa. XI.2; LXIII.10; Matth. XII.28. II. Sunt autem de Spiritu sancto quatuor potissimum probanda: 1. Revera personam esse. 2. Esse personam infinitam, seu verum Deum. 3. Esse personam a Patre et Filio procedentem. 4. Secundum hypostasin a Patre et Filio distingui.
english: CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE continued. On the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Spirit is the third person in the most holy Trinity, who emanates from the Father, is sent by the Son, and proceeds from both as distinct according to hypostasis. Spirit signifies (1) properly and adequately a being most simple and subtle in first act and essence, but in second act and efficacy most active. By singular property it is attributed to the hypostatic virtue, or third person which is in God, and that not rarely with the addition Spirit of Elohim, Spirit of the Lord, Holy Spirit — Genesis 1:2; Isaiah 11:2; 63:10; Matthew 12:28.

II. But concerning the Holy Spirit four things chiefly are to be proved: (1) that He truly is a person; (2) that He is an infinite person, or true God; (3) that He is a person proceeding from Father and Son; (4) that according to hypostasis He is distinguished from Father and Son.

source_text: VI. Secundo, Spiritum sanctum esse verum Deum ostendunt nomina divina, attributa divina, opera divina, cultus divinus. XIV. Tertio, Spiritum sanctum procedere a Patre — Joh. XV.26. XV. Procedere vero eundem a Filio — Joh. XVI.7; XX.22. Sicut enim Filius ab aeterno ex Patre generatur, ita Spiritus ab aeterno ab utroque spiratur. XVI. Discrimen vero inter generationem et processionem in modo productionis consistit. XVIII. Quarto, Spiritus sanctus non solum secundum nomen, sed et hypostasin a Patre et Filio distinguitur — Isa. XLVIII.16; LXI.1; Joh. XIV.16,26; XV.26; I Joh. V.7. Modum curiositati imponat lector, nec molestas et perplexas disputationes cupidius quam par est sibi accersat, ut pie prudenterque monet Calvinus Inst. I.13.19, et Twissus: quoties de Trinitate disserendum occurrit, cupio rem expediri quam fieri potest paucissimis. CAPUT VICESIMUM QUARTUM, De creatione in genere, sequitur.
english: VI. Secondly, that the Holy Spirit is true God the divine names, divine attributes, divine works, and divine worship show. XIV. Thirdly, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father — John 15:26. XV. And that the same proceeds from the Son — John 16:7; 20:22. For just as the Son is generated from eternity from the Father, so the Spirit is spirated from eternity from both.

XVI. But the difference between generation and procession consists in the mode of production. XVIII. Fourthly, the Holy Spirit is distinguished from Father and Son not only according to name but also according to hypostasis — Isaiah 48:16; 61:1; John 14:16,26; 15:26; 1 John 5:7.

Let the reader set a limit to curiosity, and not fetch upon himself troublesome and perplexed disputations more greedily than is fitting, as Calvin Institutes 1.13.19 piously and prudently warns, and Twisse: whenever it occurs that one must treat of the Trinity, I desire the matter to be dispatched in as few words as possible. CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR, On creation in general, follows.
